title: The role of AI assisted writing feedback in developing secondary students writing skills
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether AI-assisted writing feedback improves secondary-school English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students’ writing more than traditional teacher feedback alone. The study addresses a common instructional problem in secondary writing classrooms: teachers often cannot provide sufficiently immediate and individualized feedback because of time and workload constraints. The authors ask whether students receiving AI-generated feedback show greater gains in writing performance and also examine students’ perceptions of the AI tool.

The intervention was an 8-week classroom-based writing program in which the experimental group used Grammarly Education to receive immediate automated feedback on drafts, including grammar, spelling, punctuation, word choice, style, sentence clarity, and coherence suggestions. This was not feedback-only in a strict sense, because the AI condition also included brief teacher follow-up on higher-order concerns after AI-supported revision; thus the treatment was a hybrid AI-plus-teacher feedback model focused on revision support rather than content generation. The control group completed the same writing curriculum but received delayed traditional teacher-written feedback only. Students completed a timed persuasive essay pre-test and post-test, and weekly writing tasks across multiple genres.

Participants were 60 Turkish public high school students aged 15–17 enrolled in an intermediate-level EFL program. They were divided into experimental (n=30) and control (n=30) groups. Writing outcomes were measured using an analytic rubric adapted from the Cambridge English B2 Writing Assessment Scale with four dimensions: Content, Organization, Language Use, and Mechanics. Two independent EFL instructors scored the essays; inter-rater reliability was reported as high (Cronbach’s alpha approximately 0.89). The study also included a post-study Likert questionnaire for the experimental group to capture perceptions of the AI feedback experience.

The main conclusion is that AI-assisted feedback led to significantly greater improvement in students’ writing than teacher-only feedback. The experimental group improved from a mean of 25.8 to 32.9, compared with 25.2 to 28.6 in the control group. A mixed-design ANOVA showed a significant group-by-time interaction, F(1,58)=15.27, p<0.001, partial eta-squared=0.21, and gain scores differed significantly with a large effect size (t(58)=4.12, p<0.001, Cohen’s d approximately 1.06). The largest benefits appeared in Language Use and Organization. Students also reported favorable perceptions of the AI tool. The paper argues that AI writing feedback can effectively supplement, but should not replace, teacher guidance in secondary EFL writing instruction.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed classroom quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test control-group study with clear intervention/comparator, baseline equivalence evidence, and independent scoring, but it is not a fully described RCT and has some design/reporting concerns (single site, modest sample, limited detail on randomization and psychometrics).
impact_tier_rationale: The primary literacy outcome shows a large reported between-group effect on writing improvement (Cohen’s d≈1.06; partial η²=0.21) for a secondary-school population, indicating substantial practical impact despite the study’s methodological limitations.

interventions.use_case: Grammarly Education used as an AI-assisted writing feedback tool for Turkish secondary-school EFL students writing weekly essays; students received automated feedback on grammar, spelling, punctuation, word choice, style, clarity, and some coherence, then revised drafts with brief teacher follow-up on higher-order concerns.
Automated writing evaluation/feedback on student essay drafts during an 8-week secondary EFL writing intervention, contrasted with traditional delayed teacher-written feedback.

finding.finding_summary: In a quasi-experimental pre/post comparison with 60 Turkish high-school EFL students (experimental n=30, control n=30), the AI-assisted feedback group improved from M=25.8 (SD=5.4) to M=32.9 (SD=4.8) on a 40-point analytic writing assessment, while the teacher-feedback group improved from M=25.2 (SD=5.1) to M=28.6 (SD=5.3). The Group×Time interaction was significant, F(1,58)=15.27, p<0.001, partial η²=0.21, and gain scores favored the AI group, t(58)=4.12, p<0.001, Cohen’s d≈1.06; strongest subscore advantages were for Language Use, F(1,58)=8.92, p<0.01, and Organization, F(1,58)=4.35, p<0.05.
finding.measure: Pre-test and post-test timed persuasive essay writing scored analytically on Content, Organization, Language Use, and Mechanics using an adapted Cambridge English B2 Writing Assessment Scale; total score out of 40.
finding.std_deviation: Experimental pre SD=5.4, post SD=4.8; Control pre SD=5.1, post SD=5.3

finding.finding_summary: Post-study questionnaire responses from the experimental group (n=30) were favorable: 90% agreed the AI feedback improved their writing, 87% reported greater confidence, 83% found the feedback easy to understand and apply, and 80% wanted to continue using AI writing feedback. These findings suggest positive perceived effects on writing confidence and learner receptivity, though no validated effect size or control-group comparison was reported.
finding.measure: 5-item Likert perception questionnaire on perceived improvement, clarity of feedback, enjoyment, error awareness, confidence, and willingness to continue using AI feedback.
